Pregnancy

21 to 24 Weeks Pregnant: Baby Growth and Viability

Updated: August 5, 2026

Written and edited by Mohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama — checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

At 24 weeks pregnant, your baby is about 30 cm long, weighs around 600 g, just over a pound, and has reached the milestone many clinicians call viability. Weeks 21 to 24 bring stronger daily kicks, possibly your first Braxton Hicks contractions, and a few new items for the calendar, including the glucose screen. This guide walks through what is developing, what you may feel, and what is worth doing now.

How your baby grows from week 21 to 24

Between weeks 21 and 24, your baby puts on weight quickly, gaining more than half again what they weighed at the start of this window. At 21 weeks, most babies weigh around 350 to 400 g and measure about 26 to 27 cm from head to heel. By 24 weeks, typical estimates are close to 600 g, just over a pound, and about 30 cm, roughly the length of an ear of corn. Fat is starting to build under the skin, which still looks thin and wrinkled. Movements are more coordinated now: stretching, kicking, turning, even grabbing the umbilical cord. Many parents begin to notice a loose pattern of active and quiet periods across the day.

Two developments in this window matter a great deal. The lungs begin producing the early building blocks of surfactant, the substance that will eventually let the air sacs stay open after birth. That process continues for many weeks, which is one reason every extra week of pregnancy helps. Hearing also matures noticeably. Your baby can pick up your voice, your heartbeat, and louder sounds from outside, and may respond to them with a kick or a wriggle. Talking, reading, or singing is not required homework, but if it feels natural, this is the stage where your baby genuinely starts to listen.

What viability at 24 weeks actually means

You will often see 24 weeks described as the threshold of viability. In plain terms, it is the point where, if a baby were born extremely early, hospitals with a neonatal intensive care unit can usually offer full support, and survival becomes a realistic possibility. Chances improve meaningfully with every additional week after that. Exact outcomes vary by country, by hospital, and by the baby's own condition, so no single number applies to everyone. Some hospitals also consider active care slightly earlier in specific situations, a decision made case by case together with the family.

It helps to hold this milestone lightly. The vast majority of pregnancies continue far beyond 24 weeks, and reaching this point is not a hint that anything is about to go wrong. Think of it as quiet reassurance in the background rather than a deadline you were racing toward. The practical use of the information is simple: know which nearby hospital has newborn intensive care, keep your maternity notes easy to find, and learn the signs of preterm labor covered below so you could act quickly in the unlikely event you ever needed to.

How your body may feel in these weeks

Kicks change character in this stretch. What felt like flutters becomes unmistakable thumps, and by 24 weeks many parents feel movement every day, often strongest in the evening or after meals. You do not need to count anything formally yet; just get familiar with what a normal day of movement feels like for your baby. You may also meet Braxton Hicks contractions for the first time. These are practice tightenings of the uterus: the bump goes hard for perhaps 30 to 60 seconds, then relaxes. They are irregular, usually painless, and often triggered by activity, a full bladder, or dehydration.

Other common companions include leg cramps that strike at night, mild swelling in the ankles and feet by the end of the day, a heartier appetite, backache, and round ligament twinges when you stand up or roll over quickly. Gentle calf stretches before bed, steady water intake, putting your feet up, and supportive shoes take the edge off most of it. Swelling that is sudden, severe, or involves your face and hands is different: that deserves a same-day call to your clinician, because it can occasionally signal a blood pressure problem rather than ordinary pregnancy puffiness.

Appointments and checks in this window

From about 24 weeks, prenatal visits usually add a simple new measurement: fundal height. Your clinician or midwife runs a tape measure from the top of the pubic bone to the top of the uterus. In centimeters, the number roughly matches your week of pregnancy, give or take a couple of centimeters. It is a quick, low-tech way to confirm that growth is tracking as expected between ultrasounds. If the measurement runs noticeably ahead of or behind your dates, the usual next step is a growth ultrasound, which most of the time simply confirms that everything is fine.

This is also the moment to get your glucose screen on the calendar. Most clinics order it for the 24 to 28 week window, so if no one has mentioned it yet, ask at your next visit and book a slot that suits your schedule. Some people also have follow-up imaging if the anatomy scan could not see everything, which is common and rarely a cause for worry. Between appointments, jot down questions in BeMama or on paper as they occur to you: sleep positions, travel plans, workplace adjustments. A short written list makes a fifteen-minute visit far more useful.

Useful things to do before the third trimester

Energy is often decent in this stretch, which makes it a good season for practical projects. Start or finish the baby registry, sketch out the nursery or sleeping arrangement, and compare parental leave dates with your partner or employer. None of it has to be finished this month, but spreading the work out beats a third-trimester scramble. Keep paying casual attention to movement, too. If your baby seems clearly quieter than usual for a day, lie down on your side and pay close attention for a while; if you are still not reassured, call your clinic the same day rather than waiting.

Learn the signs of preterm labor now, while everything is calm. Call your clinic or maternity unit promptly if you notice contractions that come regularly and keep coming, perhaps four or more in an hour, a constant low backache that is new, strong pelvic or vaginal pressure, period-like cramping, a gush or steady trickle of fluid, or any bleeding. Do not wait overnight to see whether it settles, and do not worry about being wrong. Preterm labor can often be slowed or treated when it is caught early, and maternity staff would much rather check a false alarm than miss a real one.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Pregnancy is dated from the first day of the last menstrual period and is commonly described in weeks and trimesters. ACOG’s week ranges describe typical development, but they are an orientation rather than a test of an individual fetus.

Due dates are estimates, and ultrasound is used for medical reasons to assess gestational age, growth, anatomy, position, and other questions. Only a qualified prenatal professional can interpret findings for a specific pregnancy.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama’s week view for education, appointment preparation, and dated notes. It cannot confirm fetal growth, anatomy, heartbeat, or wellbeing.

When to seek help

Contact your prenatal team for bleeding, severe pain, fluid leakage, reduced movement after movement is established, or any urgent concern instead of relying on a week-by-week article.

Sources and further reading

  • ACOG — How Your Fetus Grows During Pregnancy
  • ACOG — Ultrasound Exams
  • CDC — Urgent Maternal Warning Signs and Symptoms

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Key takeaways

  • By 24 weeks your baby is about 30 cm long and just over a pound, with lungs and hearing developing fast.
  • Viability at 24 weeks is background reassurance, not a deadline; most pregnancies continue far beyond it.
  • Braxton Hicks are irregular, usually painless practice tightenings that pass with rest and water.
  • Ask at your next visit to book the glucose screen for the 24 to 28 week window.
  • Call your clinic promptly for regular tightening, pelvic pressure, leaking fluid, or bleeding.

Frequently asked questions

What symptoms are normal at 24 weeks pregnant?

Strong daily kicks, Braxton Hicks tightenings, leg cramps, mild ankle swelling, backache, and a bigger appetite are all common at 24 weeks. Most ease with water, movement breaks, calf stretches, and putting your feet up. Sudden severe swelling, regular painful contractions, bleeding, or leaking fluid are not routine symptoms and deserve a same-day call to your clinician.

Is a baby viable at 24 weeks?

Yes, 24 weeks is the point most often cited as viability, meaning a baby born this early has a realistic chance of survival with neonatal intensive care. Outcomes vary with the baby's condition and the hospital's resources, and chances improve substantially with each further week. Birth this early is uncommon, so treat the milestone as reassurance rather than a prediction.

When do Braxton Hicks contractions start?

Many people first notice Braxton Hicks contractions in the second trimester, often somewhere around weeks 20 to 24, though some feel them earlier and some never notice them at all. They are irregular, usually painless tightenings that pass with rest, a drink of water, or a change of position. Contractions that become regular, painful, or persistent before 37 weeks should be reported to your clinic promptly.

How big is a baby at 24 weeks?

At 24 weeks a baby typically measures about 30 cm from head to heel and weighs around 600 g, a little over a pound, roughly the size of an ear of corn. Ultrasound estimates carry a margin of error, and healthy babies come in a range of sizes at every week. Your clinician watches the trend over time rather than any single number.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
